frictionVectors.title: European Gas Diversification
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline gas, but accelerated diversification and renewable investment could reduce Algiers' bargaining power. Algeria is seeking long-term contracts and downstream energy partnerships to preserve leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Morocco-Sahel Strategic Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competition with Morocco and instability across the Sahel complicate Algeria's regional security posture. Border militarization and infrastructure protection continue to absorb state resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues and Chinese-backed infrastructure finance remain central to Angola's economic model, limiting policy autonomy when prices weaken or debt-service pressures rise. Western and Gulf investors are competing for influence in energy and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Corridor
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US, European, and Chinese attention because of its access to Copperbelt minerals. Expanded rail and port investment could diversify Angola, but also intensify competition over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou-Niger Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political friction with Niger continues to threaten transit revenues, energy logistics, and the viability of the Niger-Benin export corridor. Benin is seeking alternative regional trade routes while maintaining pressure on border security.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign financing and operators remain important to Cotonou port expansion, customs modernization, and energy infrastructure. These partnerships improve capacity but leave strategic logistics vulnerable to external commercial priorities.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership Tension
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pushing for greater domestic beneficiation, revenue retention, and marketing control in its diamond relationship with De Beers. Weak global diamond demand could reduce negotiating leverage and fiscal space.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, lithium, and other minerals is widening Botswana's investor base beyond diamonds. The government must balance foreign capital needs with strict licensing, environmental, and local-processing requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Nationalization
frictionVectors.details: The government is asserting tighter control over industrial mining and gold marketing while courting Russian and other non-Western partners. Weak oversight and illicit production still enable revenue leakage and elite or foreign extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Infrastructure Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence threatens mining zones, transport routes, and electricity access, increasing reliance on private security and informal supply networks. Disrupted corridors reduce the state's ability to convert mineral wealth into stable public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral prospects attract foreign operators while weak oversight and limited processing capacity reduce Burundi's control over value chains. Revenue transparency remains a persistent sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border and Transit Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain tense, complicating cross-border commerce and security coordination. Dependence on regional corridors increases Burundi's exposure to external political decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, airport, and digital infrastructure strengthens Cabo Verde's connectivity but creates leverage for external partners. The government must balance European, Chinese, and transatlantic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago's location makes it valuable for Atlantic anti-narcotics and maritime-security operations. Limited domestic enforcement capacity leaves sovereignty partly dependent on external assistance.

highlights: Oil, Gas, and Timber Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, mining, and timber sectors remain dependent on foreign technology, finance, and trading networks. Limited domestic processing and governance gaps weaken Cameroon’s ability to capture full resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and energy projects, but debt, procurement opacity, and strategic dependence complicate sovereign control over infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Access
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has expanded Moscow's political and commercial influence. Gold and diamond access remains intertwined with security arrangements and weak state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Dependence and Armed Groups
frictionVectors.details: Insecurity along routes to Cameroon and Sudan limits state control over trade, customs, and mining zones. External logistics and security partners therefore exercise outsized influence over resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure and Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily tied to oil production and export infrastructure controlled through foreign-linked operators and transit arrangements. Low diversification leaves the state vulnerable to price, contract, and pipeline pressures.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Chad is navigating reduced French influence, regional instability, and interest from Russia and Gulf actors while managing the Sudan conflict's spillover. Security partnerships can preserve regime stability but constrain independent strategic choice.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to claim Mayotte, while France maintains administrative control and a security presence there. The dispute fuels migration tensions and limits deeper bilateral cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME AND FISCAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, aid, and externally financed infrastructure, leaving limited leverage over ports, energy, and maritime resources.

highlights: Eastern security crisis threatens state control

frictionVectors.title: COBALT AND COPPER LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a dominant position in copper and cobalt processing and infrastructure-linked contracts. Kinshasa is seeking better terms and more local value addition, but bargaining power remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: M23–RWANDA PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The M23 conflict and alleged regional support continue to undermine state control in the east. Mineral smuggling, displaced populations, and competing security partnerships complicate sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-SECTOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Revenue and fiscal stability remain highly exposed to offshore oil production and international price cycles. Foreign operators and trading networks retain substantial influence over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-FOR-INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, public works, and resource-linked arrangements provide essential infrastructure but constrain fiscal flexibility and transparency.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has strengthened producer regulation and processing ambitions, but global traders and foreign manufacturers still capture much of the sector's value.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure northern communities and transport corridors. Abidjan is expanding border security and regional partnerships to protect trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti leverages its location to host US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The arrangement generates revenue and security guarantees but exposes sovereignty to major-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed port and rail infrastructure remains central to Djibouti's economy, while Ethiopia's trade dependence provides leverage. Debt, underused facilities, and competition among external operators constrain policy space.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on Gulf investment, IMF support, and foreign-currency financing is increasing outside influence over major state-linked assets and infrastructure. Suez Canal revenues remain vital but vulnerable to regional shipping disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating framework for the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dispute remains a persistent security risk despite periodic diplomatic engagement.

highlights: China remains a key infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas output is tightening fiscal space while production-sharing arrangements leave the state dependent on foreign energy companies and technical capital. Resource concentration limits economic sovereignty and diversification.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure and maritime positioning
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and investment remain important to national infrastructure, while the Gulf of Guinea's strategic location attracts wider external interest. Port and coastal assets carry both commercial and security significance.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes make it strategically relevant to Gulf states and other external powers. Port access and regional military competition increase pressure on Asmara while limiting its room for autonomous diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide essential export earnings but are dependent on foreign operators, capital, and technology. Sanctions exposure and opaque governance complicate efforts to convert mineral wealth into broader national development.

highlights: Economic sovereignty tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, remittances, transport corridors, energy links, and investment are deeply connected to South Africa, constraining Eswatini's strategic autonomy. Regional customs and labor arrangements provide stability but reinforce asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Export-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and manufacturing depend on preferential market access and external supply chains. Changes in Southern African trade rules or climate conditions could quickly affect fiscal and resource security.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy and regional leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is expanding domestic electricity capacity and strengthening Ethiopia's bargaining position, but it remains a major point of tension with Egypt and Sudan. Seasonal filling and operating arrangements continue to carry escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and dependence on international financial support limit Addis Ababa's freedom over infrastructure and macroeconomic policy. China, Gulf actors, and Western institutions all retain leverage through financing, trade, and investment.

highlights: Military transition tightens control over oil and mining

frictionVectors.title: Oil and mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value capture in oil, manganese, and other extractive sectors. Contract uncertainty could deter investment while negotiations with foreign operators continue.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains reliant on foreign capital and contractors for rail, port, and industrial infrastructure. This creates leverage for external partners over strategic logistics and resource-export routes.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty depends on regional security ties
Fisheries and port access remain strategic pressure points

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional commerce, transport corridors, and aspects of security cooperation. That dependence limits policy autonomy despite improving diplomatic normalization.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and potentially illegal fishing by foreign fleets threatens coastal livelihoods and weakens domestic control over marine resources. Enforcement capacity and licensing transparency remain persistent concerns.

highlights: Debt reforms test control over strategic resources
Gold and lithium policy seeks more domestic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pressing mining companies for stronger local procurement, processing, and fiscal returns, particularly in gold and emerging lithium projects. Foreign investment remains essential, limiting the government's negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and energy financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and financing pressures expose cocoa, petroleum, and power systems to influence from international lenders and commodity financiers. Fiscal constraints can force policies that prioritize near-term liquidity over long-term sovereign control.

highlights: Bauxite dominance expands into iron-ore ambitions
Junta centralizes control over strategic projects

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore development could transform Guinea's export capacity, but its financing, rail, and port architecture depend on large foreign consortia. The state risks gaining revenue without full control of the strategic corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and investor uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are demanding revised terms and tighter oversight across mining while delaying a clear transition to civilian rule. Political uncertainty and opaque contracting complicate both sovereignty claims and accountability.

highlights: Fragile institutions leave ports and borders exposed

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenue vulnerable to foreign traders and volatile prices. Weak bargaining power reduces national control over the principal export commodity.

frictionVectors.title: Political instability and trafficking
frictionVectors.details: Institutional rivalry and weak security capacity create openings for foreign influence, illicit trafficking, and control of maritime routes. External partners can gain disproportionate leverage through security assistance and port access.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations to China, private bondholders, and multilateral lenders constrain Nairobi's room to negotiate infrastructure and fiscal policy. Railway and port-linked financing remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia corridor offers greater strategic autonomy but faces insecurity, local land disputes, and uneven regional demand.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and related infrastructure generate vital revenue but deepen dependence on South Africa, which remains the dominant market and security partner.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Diamond revenues are vulnerable to global price cycles and foreign ownership structures, limiting domestic value capture despite the sector's importance to public finances.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled iron ore and gold operations remain central to exports, while weak processing capacity leaves Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and limited local industrial gains.

frictionVectors.title: Port Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Control over Monrovia's port and logistics systems is strategically important, with concession terms and foreign capital shaping the government's ability to retain revenue and operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed groups continue to contest oil facilities, export routes, and budget access, leaving the National Oil Corporation exposed to political coercion.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenaries and Energy Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian, and other external security relationships shape access to bases, energy infrastructure, and political influence, limiting Libya's independent control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects tied to foreign investors provide export earnings but leave Madagascar vulnerable to commodity prices, imported inputs, and disputes over taxation and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Vanilla and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and fragile ports, roads, and electricity networks reduce domestic leverage across the vanilla and mineral supply chains, despite their importance to national exports.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects, creating pressure to secure better local-benefit and processing terms. Limited state capacity weakens bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages and foreign-exchange constraints leave Malawi vulnerable to external lenders, import suppliers and regional transport disruptions. Energy insecurity directly limits industrial and agricultural sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-State Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and tighter fiscal terms, but gold production remains dependent on external operators and informal networks. Disputes risk investment delays and production disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security personnel and military cooperation has reduced Western leverage but created new dependency and reputational risks. Persistent insurgency continues to threaten mines, roads and trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal is increasing Mauritania's strategic importance, while foreign operators retain major technical and financial leverage. Revenue management and cross-border governance remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Logistics Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports depend heavily on the state rail and port system, with Chinese, Gulf and European interests competing around future infrastructure. Security risks in the wider Sahel could raise insurance and transport costs.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation Risk
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has gained diplomatic momentum, but implementation remains sensitive because of the Diego Garcia military facility and wider UK-US strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is positioning itself as an Indian Ocean logistics and services hub amid competition involving India, China and Western partners. Managing security cooperation without excessive dependence is a continuing sovereignty challenge.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is consolidating control and investment in Western Sahara while seeking wider international recognition of its autonomy plan. The dispute continues to generate regional tension, especially with Algeria and the Polisario Front.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Leverage
frictionVectors.details: EU, Gulf, Chinese and US partners are central to ports, renewables, automotive supply chains and phosphate development. Diversification strengthens Moroccan sovereignty, but strategic infrastructure remains exposed to competing outside interests.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security and LNG Access
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency continues to raise security costs and delay full-scale gas development. International security assistance protects strategic areas but increases external leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, and energy projects are central to export growth, leaving Mozambique exposed to investor priorities and debt-related constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Licensing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas prospects are drawing major international firms and could strengthen state revenues, but contract terms and local-content enforcement remain sovereignty-sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Green Hydrogen
frictionVectors.details: European and Gulf-backed projects offer capital and export access while creating risks of externally controlled infrastructure, water use, and value chains.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and oil
Western ties give way to Sahelian partnerships

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater national control over uranium and other extractive assets, creating friction with established foreign operators and raising investment uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil export infrastructure and protection of mining zones remain vulnerable to insurgency and regional isolation. Reliance on new security partners may replace one form of external leverage with another.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Control and Contract Reform
frictionVectors.details: Production recovery and licensing reforms are challenged by oil theft, pipeline sabotage, and disputes over fiscal terms. Foreign operators remain important, limiting immediate national control over upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and other external financiers are expanding roles in ports, rail, and energy. These projects improve connectivity but can create opaque obligations and competing political influence.

highlights: Mineral value chains remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and DRC Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral trading and processing ambitions face persistent scrutiny over supply-chain links to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Regional tensions threaten trade access and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, Finance, and Strategic Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The state retains strong administrative control but depends on external aid, investment, and security relationships. Suspensions or conditions imposed by donors can directly affect fiscal and infrastructure planning.

highlights: Oil prospects draw cautious external interest

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Uncertain petroleum prospects attract foreign operators seeking favorable terms, while São Tomé and Príncipe has limited capacity to negotiate and monitor complex offshore contracts.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and maritime crime threaten fisheries and shipping revenues, increasing reliance on external naval and security partnerships.

highlights: Oil and gas revenues test state capacity

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT RESET
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater domestic control and revised terms in oil, gas, and mining, creating tensions with existing investors and lenders over contract stability.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects remain dependent on foreign capital, including Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral financing, limiting Dakar's room for unilateral policy.

highlights: Island diplomacy balances India and China

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SURVEILLANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on external partners for patrol aircraft, vessels, and maritime-domain awareness against illegal fishing and trafficking, creating persistent sovereignty trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND DEBT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign access to tuna resources and continued dependence on tourism and external finance constrain the country's ability to fully capture the value of its maritime assets.

highlights: Mining drives growth but limits bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations generate export earnings but leave Sierra Leone exposed to foreign commodity cycles, investor leverage, and disputes over local benefits and environmental obligations.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, energy, and urban projects improve connectivity while increasing concerns about debt sustainability, procurement transparency, and long-term strategic dependence.

highlights: Debt relief opens limited fiscal space

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA AND PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is balancing Turkish, Gulf, Ethiopian, and Western involvement in ports and maritime security, with external access agreements directly affecting territorial sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY AND RESOURCE FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Al-Shabaab, federal-regional tensions, and contested control of fisheries and prospective hydrocarbons prevent the federal government from consistently regulating or monetizing national resources.

frictionVectors.title: Power and port bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and freight congestion continue to weaken South Africa's bargaining position in minerals and industrial supply chains. Foreign investors and trading partners are increasingly seeking direct logistical and energy safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for influence over platinum-group metals, manganese, and battery inputs. Pretoria is trying to retain downstream value while avoiding alignment with any single bloc.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and oil dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export oil depends on transit infrastructure through Sudan, leaving national revenue exposed to conflict, sabotage, and Khartoum-related bargaining. Chinese and regional oil interests retain substantial practical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External security influence
frictionVectors.details: Regional governments, international donors, and armed networks compete to shape security arrangements and political transitions. Weak institutions limit Juba's ability to convert natural-resource wealth into sovereign development.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and transport corridors

frictionVectors.title: Gold and armed-economy networks
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks use gold production and cross-border trade to finance the war. Regional intermediaries and foreign buyers reduce transparency and limit civilian control over resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and oil-export infrastructure remain strategically important but exposed to conflict disruption and external pressure. Control of logistics corridors is increasingly as important as formal ownership of assets.

highlights: Resource nationalism seeks local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors are drawing Chinese, Gulf, Indian, and Western interest. Tanzania is leveraging this competition, but long-term concessions could narrow future policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and mining control
frictionVectors.details: Natural gas, gold, and critical-mineral projects are being negotiated with stronger local-content and revenue objectives. Delays and regulatory disputes reflect the government's effort to improve terms without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's strategic port and logistics economy depend heavily on foreign capital, shipping networks, and regional transit demand. Chinese, Turkish, European, and Gulf-linked interests compete for influence over infrastructure and trade services.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector value capture
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate resources provide a core sovereign asset, but processing capacity and market access remain vulnerable to external technology, finance, and commodity cycles. The government is seeking greater domestic value addition while managing fiscal pressures.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European cooperation on migration, trade, and budget support gives Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance to perceived external conditionality constrains the government's room to maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Imported energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and electricity bottlenecks, leaving energy security sensitive to European interconnection and external financing.

highlights: China and Gulf capital expand reach

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: The oil project has strengthened state ambitions for resource control but depends heavily on foreign operators, lenders, and transit infrastructure. Western environmental and financial pressure complicates execution while increasing reliance on non-Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-influence competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and regional investors compete for influence through roads, energy, and logistics projects. Debt-service obligations and opaque contracting can narrow Uganda's bargaining power over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking more revenue, local processing, and stronger oversight, but foreign firms still dominate capital-intensive mining and export channels. Competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors gives Lusaka leverage but also raises risks of regulatory concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Transport corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports depend on vulnerable rail and road routes through neighboring states. New corridor financing can diversify access, but it may also create long-term dependence on external infrastructure sponsors.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese dominance in critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese companies remain central to Zimbabwe's lithium and broader mineral investment, providing capital while reinforcing an export-oriented model. Local beneficiation rules improve formal sovereignty but have limited effect without reliable power, finance, and processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment-system isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance raise transaction costs and push Harare toward alternative partners. This reduces external scrutiny but strengthens the bargaining position of lenders and investors willing to operate in a high-risk environment.
